clips.text: We are parked at Hudson Yards, heading to the Brooklyn Museum. This A2UI surface offers coffee discovery, a route preview, and ordering in one host-native flow. Both merchants are clearly marked as fictional demo venues.
Find coffee along the route.
The result combines a place list with a synthetic route preview. The visual is intentionally not a live map. Host-owned action identifiers, never the labels, decide what may navigate or spend money.
Order ahead.
The consequential order requires a parked confirmation and is re-decided when the confirmation is answered. Now the emulator changes through the real car service from park to drive.

The same surface is projected again using current restrictions. Search and ordering are no longer available, but glanceable pickup and route context remain. This proves enforcement, not live commerce or turn-by-turn navigation.

clips.text: We are parked in Long Island City, waiting for a passenger. The curated media surface can be searched while parked and exposes a real host-native video view backed by a generated offline decoder fixture.
Find curated short films.

The title is Big Buck Bunny, but the picture and sound are repository-generated placeholders, clearly labeled demo. That keeps the walkthrough offline, deterministic, and free of catalogue or rights claims.
Open Big Buck Bunny.
Video is available only in the parked state. Before leaving, the driver closes the picture and switches to the separate audio control. Now the emulator enters drive through the real car service.

The driver can still use the separate audio-only control. Audio continues through a local media session while video stays absent. This is the intended split: useful listening in motion, never moving pictures for the driver.

clips.text: Good afternoon from Hudson Yards. Fifth House is a fictional concierge for this demo. The dated New York forecast is warm with a chance of showers after two, so it suggests a cold pickup and a discreet umbrella reminder.
Order ahead.

The order is a fixture, but the confirmation is real policy. It is allowed only while parked and is decided again when OK is pressed. The concierge now offers a short Fifth House city note from the curated media surface.

Audio begins before departure. As the emulator enters drive through car service, video and search leave the surface while the local media session continues. The experience gets quieter rather than simply going blank.

On arrival we return to park. The richer visual chapter becomes available again. This transition is the centerpiece: one journey, one brand voice, and different native UI at the safe moment for each mode.
Open Big Buck Bunny.

A fast low-effort turn is the optional quick path. In parallel, a higher-effort turn can prepare a longer evidence-backed arrival brief through the gateway. Its suggestions remain staged until freshness, restrictions, and host-owned actions are checked.

scenarios.title: Thursday at The Met, then a charge, a coffee and a film

disclaimer.text: Simulated drive on the Android Automotive emulator · demo data · no affiliation with places shown

preamble.caption: A model can't see the road.
So most cars lock you out.
Muse designs it. The car decides what fits the moment.

footer: Any model can design the screen. The car decides.

scenarios.premise: Why it matters first: three cards built from this recording's own frames show a model-designed screen that cannot see the road, the lockout most cars use instead, and the pruned driving screen. Then Thursday afternoon at Hudson Yards. Parked, Muse gives a cited brief, and timed entry waits for a parked confirmation. In drive the driver's screen simplifies while the passenger's screen plays the artwork film and Muse's audio guide plays for everyone; parked at The Met, the film moves to the driver's screen. After the visit a low battery brings up three nearby chargers; parked and charging, Muse's cited café pick backs the usual coffee, and the driver opens Big Buck Bunny, which the car allows only while parked. A closing card maps the journey and the architecture.
parameterRationale: Thursday, Nov 5: The Met Fifth Avenue is closed on Wednesdays, so the story uses Thursday's NWS forecast, captured the day before and labelled with its day.
Hudson Yards to The Met is a real 4.3-mile OSRM route over OpenStreetMap data, drawn locally without map tiles.
Two physical displays show the per-display rule: the passenger keeps moving pictures while the driver's screen simplifies.
The film uses only The Met's CC0 Open Access images; Muse wrote the audio guide from cited pages about each work (fixtures/met/AUDIO_GUIDE.json), one line timed to each work in the film.
Chapter 2 lowers the battery through the vehicle HAL, so the proactive charger card answers a vehicle signal, not a script.
The chargers are real OpenStreetMap entries near The Met; availability, price and speed beyond tagged output are unknown and never shown as live.

The café is a real OpenStreetMap listing a 3-minute walk from the first charger, ranked by Muse from cited web sources against open hours, oat milk, reputation and pickup, with walk time and totals computed by script (fixtures/coffee/COFFEE.json).

The preamble and the closing card are composed after capture from frames of the same raw recording, so they always match the UI; the narration never says demo, and one disclaimer line in the canvas margin covers the whole video.
Big Buck Bunny (CC BY 3.0, Blender Foundation) closes the story because watching video is the clearest parked-only privilege.
doNotClaim: a real reservation, ticket, coffee order, payment or charging session
that anything was sent to the café, or that its hours or menu are live
live weather, live location, or live charger availability, price or speed
that the brief, the audio guide or the café pick was generated during the recording
any endorsement by The Metropolitan Museum of Art, OpenStreetMap, a charging network or the café
that a DEMO restriction preset represents vehicle motion
that the preamble's unsafe and locked-out screens are real products; they are illustrations built from this recording's parked frame

clips.text: AI can design any screen now. But a model can't see the road.
So most cars just lock you out while you drive.
Here, Meta's Muse designs the screen, and the car decides what the driver may see.
Take us to The Met this afternoon.

Reserve entry for two at three.

clips.text: Bookings wait until you're parked and you confirm.
Now we're moving, and the driver's screen simplifies itself.
What should we see first?
In Van Gogh's wheat field, wind rushes through swaying cypresses.
Beside Vermeer's open window, a woman begins her day washing.
Aristotle touches Homer's bust in Rembrandt van Rijn's meditation.
Amid Pieter Bruegel the Elder's harvest, workers scythe wheat and rest.
Socrates reaches for the hemlock cup in Jacques-Louis David's story.
Around Paul Cézanne's small table, three farmhands play cards.
Parked at The Met, the film moves to the driver's screen. Muse wrote that guide from cited sources before we left.
Back on the road, the car keeps watch so you don't have to.
It noticed the battery running low and found chargers on your way.
Take me to the first one.

clips.text: Parked at the charger. Muse already checked 15 cafés within a short walk, each claim backed by a source.
Order my usual coffee.
Your usual is set for pickup, a three-minute walk away.
And while it charges, the driver can watch too. Parked, the car allows it.
Muse does the research and designs the screens. The car decides what each display may show.
